estimate: no NASA number for a suited walking slope was found; the patch itself (HiRISE at 1 m) is never steeper than 25 degrees, so 25 keeps every real slope walkable and steeper rock faces climbable only by the step row

estimate: no NASA number found; a heavy electric vehicle on loose ground reaching the SEV's ~2.8 m/s (10 km/h, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/464826main_sev_factsheet_508.pdf) in about 3 to 9 s
rows.note: value at the top of the range (Ravindu's playtest of 13 Nov 2026: "I felt the rover is slow"): 0 to top speed in 2.8 s. Still an estimate, not a measured rover number

rows.source: estimate: the SEV's wheels "pivot 360 degrees", so it can turn on the spot (https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/464826main_sev_factsheet_508.pdf); a slow pivot of 10 to 30 degrees a second, no measured rate found

Curiosity rolls over obstacles up to 65 cm on 0.5 m wheels, 1.3 wheel diameters (JPL MSL fact sheet, https://solarsystem.nasa.gov/docs/MSL%20Fact%20Sheet%20REV-141119.pdf); the Apollo LRV was built to climb a 35 cm step on 81.8 cm tyres, 0.43 diameters (UMD ENAE 788X LRV case study slide 47, https://spacecraft.ssl.umd.edu/academics/788XF20/788XF20L05.LRVx.pdf). For the SEV's 0.99 m wheels (active suspension, no number published): 0.43 to 1.29 m. Excerpts: design/research/pages/rover-climb/excerpts.md
rows.note: the tallest rock or step a wheel rolls up onto (sandbox/rover.gd); a static whose top is no higher than this over its underside (a build pad, a sill: world.gd _solidify()) is ground to a wheel as a rock is. Taller ones stop the rover. Value: the wheel's radius, under the chassis's 0.62 m clearance, so a rock the wheels climb never meets the belly

rows.source: estimate: a wheel brakes at most at its traction, mu x g; dry loose sand gives mu of about 0.3 to 0.6 (no rover measurement found) and Mars g is 3.71 m/s2 (world.gravity row): 1.1 to 2.2 m/s2. Value at the low end, so the rover rolls to a stop at a rock instead of lurching

NASA's Lunar Electric Rover (the SEV's forerunner): interior volume 10.8 m3, net habitable volume about 8.6 m3, crew of two for 14 days (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20100009798, design/research/pages/sizes/ntrs-20100009798.txt). Value: the cabin's cut-out inside, printed by forge/vehicle_rover.py

estimate: the SEV is 3.05 m tall (fact sheet, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/464826main_sev_factsheet_508.pdf) on a chassis listed as 1.3 m tall (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Exploration_Vehicle, citing NASA's LER fact sheet), so the cabin is at most about 1.75 m outside; 10.8 m3 inside over a floor of about 2.2 x 3 m is about 1.6 m
rows.note: floor to ceiling inside (forge/vehicle_rover.py FLOOR to ROOF). The seated suited hero needs 1.57 m from boots to helmet (measured in drive_sit); the real crew ride without suits, which wait on the suitports

rows.source: estimate: a leaf or romaine lettuce head at harvest is commonly 20 to 35 cm across; the saved NASA Veggie paper (NTRS 20190028955) gives days to harvest, not size

Apollo crews 70 to 80+ steps a minute (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html); a suited 1 g treadmill study 88.8 steps/min (design/research/suit.md, Cullinane 2017). Value: walk speed / half the stride
two steps; Apollo 16 3.4 to 4.6 ft per stride (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html) and Cullinane 2017 1.243 m (design/research/suit.md); value = 1.0 m/s / 1.5 steps/s x 2
estimate: Apollo 16 fastest about 105 steps a minute (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html); no Mars-gravity measurement
peak knee flexion suited in reduced gravity, read off a graph (Norcross et al. 2010, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20110003409, Fig. 26): about 60 unsuited
feet apart while walking suited: Cullinane 2017 and Apollo 15 video (design/research/suit.md)
suited walk-to-run transition, Froude 0.36 +/- 0.11 over 38 Apollo gait events (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2719915/)
derived: 2 x 1.17 m/s / 3.73 m/s2, the Apollo 16 take-off speed under Mars gravity (see hero.jump.hop)
forward lean of suited crew bending to pick things up, Apollo 16 (https://www.nasa.gov/history/alsj/a11/a11.gaits.html; design/research/suit.md)
estimate: a foot counts as landed within 2 cm of the floor; a check on footstep timing, not a feel number

estimate: Armstrong on the Moon, 'I only go in a small fraction of an inch, maybe an eighth of an inch' (3 mm at 1/6 g; ALSJ 109:24:48, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/static/history/alsj/a11/a11.step.html); Viking Lander 1 footpad 3 went 0.036 m into blocky ground (Moore et al. 1987, USGS PP 1389). A boot weighs 2.3 times as much on Mars (0.38 g against 0.166 g), so about 1 cm. Excerpts: design/research/pages/sinkage/excerpts.md
rows.note: how far a planted boot sits in the dust: the drawn hero is this much lower than its collider

rows.note: a lander's footpad: tonnes on four plates

rows.source: estimate: no measured buried share found; Viking 1 pictures show blocks 'partly buried by sediment' (NASA SP-425, https://solarviews.com/history/SP-425/ch21.htm, search summary only). A rounded block shows its widest middle, and the undercut below it reads as a gap, unless about a third of its height is in the ground

Floor: NASA VIPER, the fastest planetary rover, 'top speed 20cm/s, nominal speed 10 cm/s' (https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20240013903); Curiosity 4 cm/s, Spirit and Opportunity 5 cm/s. Ceiling: robots that drive among people, Pudu BellaBot 'Safety Speed: 0.5-1.2 m/s (Adjustable)' (https://www.pudurobotics.com/en/products/bellabot), Starship delivery robot 'around average walking speed (6kmph)' (https://collection.sciencemuseumgroup.org.uk/objects/co8697500/starship-technologies-self-driving-delivery-robot). Saved: design/research/pages/pip/
rows.why: PIP is a helper that potters among the crew and leads a new commander round the base, not a science rover: a robot built to drive among people, at a walking pace a little above the hero's walk (hero.speed.walk 1.0), so a walking kid following it never catches it and steps on it (13 Nov playtest: at 0.5 m/s the kid did)

rows.source: estimate: no small-rover figure found; 0.8 m/s2 reaches PIP's 1.1 m/s in 1.4 s, quick enough to pull away from a hero walking into it and still a soft start (an indoor service robot's, not measured)
estimate: skid-steered small robots turn in place in a few seconds; 60 deg/s is a half turn in 3 s, slow enough to read as looking round (not measured)
